children.text: This is democracy, a podcast that explores the interracial, intergenerational and intersectional unheard voices living in the world's most influential democracy.
Welcome to our new episode of this is democracy.

This week's episode focuses on one of the most discussed topics in politics today, but also one that's often misunderstood, campaign finance and the role of money in American politics in general and in particular in political campaigns.
And we have with us probably the person who's thought about these issues most deeply that I know, Brian Roberts.
He's a professor here at the University of Texas in Austin, a friend and colleague in the Department of Government.
Brian studies American political institutions, interest groups and positive political economy, which basically means that being an expert on political science was not enough for him.
He also wanted to be an expert on economics.

And so he studies the intersection between economics and politics, which is what allows him to have a unique understanding of the role of money in politics, really getting into the economic elements of it in a way that most of us who are not trained in that field can't.
He writes on a wide variety of fields.
I recommend his articles on politics and financial markets, corporate political participation and distributive politics.
Brian, welcome to the podcast.
It's so good to be here.
Thank you.
Thank you for taking the time.
Before we turn to our discussion with Brian, we have, of course, Zachary's scene setting poem.
What's the title of your poem today?
Money Have Mercy.
Money Have Mercy.
Let's hear it.
Money, how naive you were when you were little bits of gold that changed hands in Egypt millennia ago.
How innocent when we used to preserve you in our ceramic pink pigs to buy balloons and bazooka bubble gum.
And the way I used to collect state quarters like they weren't just the zinc leftovers of cash thrown at endless politicians and improbable gerrymandered districts.
The way Asheville, North Carolina has no Democratic representatives.
And it's easy to become despondent thinking of you, of the streets paved with gold that my great grandparents never truly found.
The way it all seems so useless, idly thumbing the softened sheets of green paper in my old wallet the way the coins just pile up on the counter.
But I have always lived in state capitals defined by state capital, freedom havens defined by free markets.
And money, you have made America somewhat of a contradiction.
The ultimate mixed economy, diverse society that still clings to the extremes like a clothesline.
The way hundreds of thousands of dollars are needed just to have a say in this city.
The way that there are whole logistical organizations hellbent on buying democracy, still proselytizing religion as they sell despondency.
Money, greenbacked buyer of all things, where were you yesterday for the homeless man under the 183 overpass?
And what will you do to our country, still 350 days before the election?
Whatever it is, have mercy on our pocketbooks.
That's wonderful, Zachary.
I love the playfulness of that.
And I love the contradictions that you capture.
What is your poem really about?
My poem is really about how much money defines our society in both good and bad, and how much of a role it has in our politics today.
A big role, you see.
Yeah.
A very big role.
That's, I think, the perfect place to turn to Brian.
You've thought about this so much, Brian.
How do we understand the role of money in politics?
Where does it come from in our society?
Well, I mean, money has been part of American politics from the very beginning.
Early on, it was very much sort of inside politics money.
The candidates themselves would fund their campaigns.
And then you get the Jacksonian democratization, if you will.
And that changed things a little bit.
I think one of the interesting historical turning points, ironically, was the Pendleton Act in 1883, when it kind of overthrew the way that money had been raised, which was through the party systems.
And suddenly that was done away with.
The spoil system was effectively done away with.
This creates a modern civil service system.
But that was the way parties funded politics back then.
You paid to have a position in government.
And then, well, we still need money to fund some of these things.
And that's where people like Mark Hanna got creative.
And like any good bank robbers, ask the question, why did you rob the banks?
That's where the money is, right?
So where did Mark Hanna go?
He went to the corporations.
So Mark Hanna was the fundraiser and political organizer for President William McKinley.
Exactly.
And this coincides, of course, with industrialization in this country and the rise of these large corporate entities for which there was no precedent.
And there was also sort of no precedent for the amount of money that they potentially had.

And so that kind of got a lot of the stuff kicked off and ultimately led to a lot of the progressive era reforms with the passage of the first federal campaign finance act in 1907 with the Tillman Act, which clamped down on corporate contributions.
And off we went from there.
But it was still possible at that time for wealthy individuals like John D. Rockefeller to make huge contributions.
Absolutely.
Absolutely.
And that was where both parties actually were going early on.
One of the ironies of history there was there was a lot of the two early things that people talked about in terms of regulating money.
One was corporate contributions and the other was disclosure.

And the disclosure turned out to be more of a challenge for the political class than the corporate contribution ban, because like you suggested, there were other means by which you could tap into some large amounts of money.
But one of the ways that disclosure got going was in 1908 election when Taft against William Jennings Bryan announced that he was unilaterally going to disclose all his contributions.
And then Bryan went along with that as well.
And this was before any law had passed.
And it turned out to be this political coup because it turned out that the large individual donors backed way off.
And so when he in fact did disclose all this money, that it was nowhere near where people thought it would be.
And this was considered a big plus for Taft and he ends up winning the election.
So people didn't have as much money from rich people as people thought.
And as a consequence, he had to begin thinking about small donors in ways that had never been thought before.
And then two years later, Congress gets on board and starts passing the first disclosure laws and we're off and running.
I see.
And did that empower the parties at that point or?
Well, the parties were struggling because they were still trying to settle on a new funding model.
And so there was still a lot of reliance on East Coast money.
This was another thing that we began to see the first efforts to broaden the donor base.
And the Republicans under George Perkins put out the first sort of direct mail and reached out across the country to small business owners and asked them for $50 a piece.
And got 50% response rate, which was pretty extraordinary.
And Democrats were largely relying on party newspapers and then soliciting through them and weren't doing quite as well.
And when we think about the Great Depression and World War II, did this kind of fundraising stop in that period or what happened?
No, I think, well, obviously that period saw the rise of organized labor, which became a political force and ultimately led Congress to clamp down on them under a lot of the World War II legislation.
And part of that clamping down had to do with money in politics.
And one of the interesting historical facts there is in response to several pieces of legislation there, most notably Smith-Connolly Act, organized labor created the first political action committee.
Called the Political Action Committee.
And again, we're off and running.
So they invented this.
They invented it as a way of dealing with some of the restrictions that Congress was putting on them.
So it was to raise money separately, not use union funds directly to make independent expenditures and the like.
Because the concern was that labor unions owned certain candidates.
So this was a way of trying to at least create some distance between the AFL-CIO and a particular candidate at the time.
Is it fair to say that this system though, as it came into existence, was part of the story of Franklin Roosevelt's revolution?
Was he one of the chief beneficiaries of this?
Well, certainly of the rise of organized labor, right?
And that's, you know, so some of the things that happened during World War II that didn't sit well with Congress was tied to organized labor.
But it was also, so, but they carried it over to all sorts of other things such as campaign finance.
Okay.
But yeah, I mean, that was an interesting era.
But, you know, in terms of the underlying regulations, there was a Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925 that was sort of the last major campaign finance law until the 70s.
And you know, it's kind of a well-known, well-trod story that no one ever got hurt by the Federal Corrupt Practices Act.
Right, right.
One of the things you and I have talked about is how hard it is to enforce even the limited restrictions that exist.
And at that time, there was no independent enforcement agency, no Federal Election Commission.

The disclosures was turned over to the House and the Senate and was on paper and ended up in some dark closet, which is, you know, there were some intrepid political scientists that dug into that, but not a whole lot of work was done with that.
And is the period after World War II the beginning of what we see today?
Would you link that to today, or?
Yeah.

I mean, what's interesting about campaign finance regulation is all the ideas were talked about early on in the 20th century, the limits on contributions, expenditures, disclosure, even public funding was mentioned pretty early on.

And so, you know, one of the interesting history lessons here is the sort of the absence of new ideas or sort of the same, the contours of campaign finance regulation have largely remained the same, just sort of variations on some very old themes.
How have we really seen, like, how is money played differently in a politics that is increasingly defined by the media and by technology?
Well, so first thing about money in politics is by far and away, most of the money raised, most of money spent goes through the media.
It's for political advertising of one form or another.
So there's a direct connection between media and money there, right?
That's always been there in terms of how the money is used.

You know, it's gotten more interesting now with social media and, you know, now some of the First Amendment discussions are bleeding over to the private sector and sort of all the discussions with Facebook and Google and Twitter, which is largely outside the reach of the First Amendment in terms of campaign finance regulation.
But debating about who can speak how much, about what, and who regulates that, right?

And it's largely something that's been untouched, at least in some sense, by federal law, but it's something now being debated within private actors, which is a very interesting new wrinkle to all that entire debate.
And it's a controversy, of course, that goes back to radio and television, which I think was Zachary's question.
So certainly the rise of radio, in particular television in the 60s, significantly raised the cost of campaigning.
And that's really what led to the first new campaign finance laws, early 1970s, 1971, which replaced the 1925 law.

But it was designed primarily to deal with rising campaign costs and the fact that the Democratic Party was emerging from the 60s in pretty significant deficit and trying to figure out some way to control things, control costs.
And is that also the moment that we should start talking about, at least the perception that corporations are more significant?
I mean, Lyndon Johnson, of course, mobilizes Brown and Root and other oil money in Texas.
You get these isolated stories.
I mean, clearly, one of the things that's sometimes lost on history is how much the Watergate scandal was a campaign finance scandal.
Yes, absolutely.
And that included some very large individual donations, but also some corporate contributions that came to light and which were illegal, right?
But because those contributions have been outlawed since 1907, but nonetheless, it reemerges on the front pages as an issue again.
Sure, sure.
And it was really Watergate and the 1974 amendments to that 1971 bill, which was in the large course of history, pretty innocuous.
It was trying to control campaign costs.
The 74 amendments in the wake of Watergate were really set the framework for modern campaign finance.
And so then how should we think about today?
That history is super, I think, important in understanding where we are today, right?
How would you define or describe the landscape for people?
Well, the landscape, again, gets defined by Watergate and the 74 amendments and then the subsequent court challenge, which ended up in a very, very significant court case, Buckley versus Vallejo.
Right, we should talk about that for the next couple of minutes.
And, you know, the biggest thing about Buckley is it created explicitly the...one of the frameworks created there was that any debate about money in politics was about the First Amendment.
Right, it's a 1976 Supreme Court case.
Exactly.
And so the court starts its procurium unsigned decision, noting that...and this is something of a misnomer, the notion that they said money equals speech.
They basically made a very pragmatic observation.
In today's day and age, mid-70s, it costs a lot of money to engage in mass communication, political communication.
And so if you limit money in politics, you are effectively limiting speech, political speech in a democracy.
And they went to great pains to say, you know, this isn't any kind of speech.
This is really important stuff.
And so that has been the foundation for all discussions ever since.
It revolves around this First Amendment question, and then it's debates about to what extent one can limit what would otherwise be an infringement on the First Amendment.
And those debates have been raging ever since.
And Buckley was instrumental.
Nobody likes the Buckley decision.

One of the things it did that is most controversial...I mean, I think casting it in terms of the First Amendment set some people off, but the big compromise, the big political compromise in Buckley was using that framework, the First Amendment framework, and what criteria or, as it turns out, criterion would be...needed to be met in order to infringe on the First Amendment, if you will.
And that turned out to be corruption or the perception of corruption.
Now, there were some other ideas advanced, including one of equalization, which resonates with a lot of people, but the court emphatically says, we're not going there.
It's not something we really want to entertain at all.
And so we're left with a framework that says, if you limit money in politics, you are infringing on the First Amendment.
However, much like you can't...you can pass laws that say you can't scream fire in a movie theater unless, in fact, there is a fire.
So the compelling interest that the court came up with was corruption or the appearance of corruption.
And that has...that led to the next really controversial part of the decision, which was using that framework, the court decides that contribution limits are constitutional.
They are okay.
They used a lower level of scrutiny in evaluating contribution limits.
These are contributions to candidates.
To candidates, to political action, well, to parties.
There were several provisions in there, but principally, the Buckley case was about individual contributions.
And so limits on contributions were okay, but limits on expenditures were not okay.
And so that was sort of splitting the baby in ways that satisfied nobody.
So either those that wanted more wholesale limits on money in politics or those that wanted to abandon that enterprise altogether.
And so...but this compromise, this political truce in some sense, has endured, right?
We have kept to that very fine line created in Buckley to this day.
And everyone operates both with this notion that contribution limits are okay.
There's lots of court battles over what those boundaries are, but the principle has remained.
But that expenditure limits, not okay.
Now Buckley talked about expenditure limits in the context of individuals and didn't entertain discussion of expenditures by others, in particular corporations or unions.
And that's what subsequently comes up in Citizens United in 2010.
But the one thing about Citizens United is it really offers no new language other than that was found in Buckley in 1976.

There was a court case in 1990 that actually upheld laws that banned corporate independent expenditures, a case out of Michigan, Austin versus Michigan Chamber, that stayed within the Buckley framework and found, even though Buckley had said no limits on expenditures, found a way to uphold a law limiting or prohibiting corporate independent expenditures.
But we won't go into the details of that, but Citizens United basically restores the argument, the principles established and the definitions established back in Buckley.
And so Citizens United didn't break a whole lot of new ground in that sense.
So the playing field really from 76 is that there are limits on what any of us can give to a particular federal candidate if there's a federal statute passed, and of course there is.
And that can also apply in other domains as well, such as Austin races, and Austin have limits on them as well.
But there cannot be any limit on how much a candidate can spend.
Candidate can spend or a third party.
Or a third party, which is where we get into political action committees and other groups.
And in particular, what we call super PACs, which are limited to making what are called independent expenditures, right?
So these are political ads that expressly advocate for or against a named candidate, but lack any coordination or communication with a party or a candidate.
And that's the world we live in, in many ways right now.
Great.
And this is so helpful in answering this question, which I think is really our money question, which is what's the real problem then today?
Why is it that it appears that money, in particular in the last 20 to 30 years, has skewed our elections?
And of course, as you've pointed out, it's always been a part of our elections.
Yeah.
And that's a really interesting question.
I actually have my undergraduates do a research project every year addressing the question of whether money buys election outcomes.
And you can ask Hillary Clinton whether that matters.
You can ask Beto O'Rourke whether money buys elections.
It's not uniformly the case.

And in fact, some of the very early research using data that was first released in the mid-'70s, late-'70s by the Federal Election Commission, you found some perverse findings where the more incumbents spent, the lower their vote share.
Wow.
Well, that was on aggregate.
And that actually reflected the fact that often when incumbents spend a lot of money, it's when they're in trouble.
Okay.
And sometimes they don't win.
So you get these very odd kinds of findings when you look at these things in aggregate.
So it's not a guarantee, right?
But it is a barrier for many, is it not?
A barrier, yeah.
I mean, you have to raise money, right?
I think in 2018, the average winning Senate campaign was about $15 million.
That's a lot of money.
But even then, that obscures the fact that a lot of those weren't as contested as others.
So Beto O'Rourke spent $80 million not winning an election, right?

But you still, you know, Senate campaigns, you know, you're talking in the tens of millions potentially, you know, House campaigns, you know, three to five million kind of is sort of a winning campaign total.
And for House, it's even more of a challenge because those are happening every two years.
And you know, one of the big concerns that people raise about raising money by House members is it never ends.

And House members spend an inordinate amount of time raising money rather than doing perhaps what the people want them to do, which is to legislate and meet with them and discuss and ponder bigger issues.

And so that's led to some really interesting reform proposals, you know, why don't we loosen up the contribution limits on federal candidates in order to free them up to actually spend time with us, right?
I mean, one mechanism people have tried to do that over the years, of course, is through public funding.
And certainly at the federal level, first of all, there was never a public funding system for Congress.
And the presidential one is basically evaporated.
Because the candidates can raise more money on their own rather than following the rules.
I mean, Barack Obama in 08, you know, was facing maybe getting $94 million from the presidential campaign fund and compare that to the close to a billion dollars you could raise on your own.
And it was at that point a no-brainer.
And we've never looked back on that.
But does your close look at the data indicate that the fundraising is giving inordinate influence to certain groups?
I mean, is that a fear?
So the influence question is one of the real challenges in social science, right?
So people have looked for relationships between contributions by, say, corporate PACs and votes in Congress.
And they don't find that to be a systematically positive relationship, right?
It turns out to be difficult to get that linkage.
And people have taken those findings and say, well, you're just not measuring the right thing, which is a good point.
But then the question is, how do you begin to measure that kind of thing?
And people have talked in terms of access, which I've always found a bit odd because do you want access simply for the purpose of access or do you want access for policy?
And but, you know, people have looked at whether this campaign contributions by corporate PACs have led either to policy and they've had a challenge there.
Or do firms that do that, do they see a particular bump in their earnings or stock prices, all sorts?
And it just doesn't seem to be there.
So one of the challenges in this debate where we're all thinking that, you know, corporations are in particular are taking advantage of this is they're really the evidence isn't there systematically.

And and, you know, I've argued that all the attention that people have paid, particularly on to corporate money in politics, is probably a little misplaced
because corporations, for a lot of reason, don't have an incentive to participate in
politics, particularly to take advantage of the freedoms allowed under Citizens United,
because that would that allowed corporations to pay for ads that said, you know, vote for
this candidate.
Well, that candidate has a party label.
And as soon as a corporation does that, you've basically alienated half the country.
And it just from a corporate strategy point of view, doesn't make any sense.

And and there were there was an amicus brief submitted to both in the case of Citizens United and an earlier case from a large business group that said, look, this isn't this is great, but we don't want it.
Right.
And we're not going to take advantage of this.
Why?
Why would we do that?
Right.
Now, that that applies more rigorously, I think, to large public face, consumer facing publicly traded firms.
Right.
Where it gets a little more difficult is privately held firms.

And and I think particularly when you get off the national scene and you start looking at state and local elections, that would think that's that's much more likely where something like that will emerge.
It's just hard to document it systematically.
Right.
Right.
Right.
But most of the money, I think you said in a conversation with me before, about 95 percent comes from individuals.
Oh, yeah.
No, absolutely.
And, you know, you look at the, you know, 2018, the 10 largest super PACs.
Right.
You go look at where they got their money, you know, over 92 percent from individuals whose names were disclosed.
Right.
Right.

And even that's a little bit skewed because there were a couple that dropped down into the high 60 percent or something like that, that that drug down the the normal rate, which was close to 98 percent or more.
Right.
So and what's the weighting of big and small donations?
Is it well, this is so if you're itemized, these are the ones I'm talking about where where names are revealed, along with your occupation and home addresses and all that sort of good stuff.
It's if you give two hundred dollars, more than two hundred dollars.
Right.
Then you're obligated to to report this sort of stuff.
Right.
And so so all of all the super PAC stuff is effectively disclosed.
I mean, certainly, you know, we hear a lot about dark money and the potential for corporations to and they certainly can.
That's a way in which corporations can remain and individuals can remain anonymous.
And this is going through what we call 501 C four fives and sixes of 501 C fours are called social welfare organizations.
And that that's the principal mechanism that's associated with dark money because the donors to a 501 C four do not have to be disclosed.
They were historically disclosed to the IRS in 2018.
The IRS said we don't want that information.
But then a court said not so fast.
So that's a little bit in limbo.
So that's disclosed.
But to the IRS, but not publicly until things get settled there.
But but the amount of corporate money in there is is debatable.
Right.
And there's partly a reason it's debatable.
Some of those privately disclosed forms to the IRS have actually found their way in into the sunlight.

And between that and there were a couple of very important cases where one of these organizations was was sued and actually the FEC, the Federal Election Commission, was sued to to redesignate one of these things is what they call a political committee, which would be subject to the Federal Election Commission regulation that would have required more disclosed full disclosure.

And there was a 501 C for one of these social welfare organizations that actually, as part of their agreement with the FEC, agreed to be reclassified as a political committee and then fully disclosed their donors.
And the same thing happened to a 501 C six, which was a trade association.
A lot of people who had given money to that trade association under the assumption of anonymity suddenly found themselves quite publicly disclosed.
And so I think going forward, there's going to be a tremendous amount of caution, believe in believing that that actually will be or remain anonymous.
And again, the fundamental point is that most of this money is coming from individuals.
It's not coming from, again, the dark money stuff, the 501 C's we don't know.
Right.
We can guess we can understand the incentives for some to remain anonymous.
But, you know, when they are exposed, yeah, there's some corporate money there.
But the bigger money is individuals.
Right.
Zachary?
Yeah.
So a lot of people are expressing concern that there's too much money in politics and whether their concerns are evidence based or not.
It's a big problem when a lot of people don't believe in the soundness of our institutions.
So what do you think are the solutions to at least in the minds of the public level, the playing field?
Well, I mean, this is this is this whole debate about whether equalization versus liberty, where you fall on that spectrum becomes an issue.
I mean, this is the the question of sort of equal voice is.
That's what you mean by equalization.
Yeah.
Mechanisms that are designed to do that.
I mean, public funding does that to some extent.
But, you know, early on, there were expenditure limits.
On candidates in particular.
And and but the courts have have not been particularly happy with that.
So right now, there is really no.
Reason to believe that the courts will back off in any way from what effectively are unlimited independent and independent expenditures.
And so, you know, we see initiatives, public funding initiatives, particularly at the state and local level.
Now, you know, Seattle has a very famous one.
But, you know, Maine and Arizona have had statewide public funding initiatives.
That's all well and good, but they cannot deal with independent expenditures.
There was an effort in Arizona to try and wrap in independent expenditures as part of a public funding system.
But that was overturned by the by the Supreme Court not too long ago, 2011.
So what would you do, though?
I mean, obviously, we have to deal with the realities of our system as it is.
But but you're I mean, you've you've studied and mastered the detail.

What are the ways we could turn the details to at least create a more of a perception of fairness, but be also to to at least give more of a shot to those who, for whatever reasons, have more trouble getting access to money?
Yeah.
You know, the opening.
So the biggest constraint are the courts.
Right.
I mean, that's one of the things that people fully don't appreciate is is Congress has done surprisingly little.
Surprisingly, though, even knowing Congress, they've done they introduce a lot of bills, but they almost by design don't go very far.
As you've said to me before, these are the winners of the system.
Of course.
No, no, no.
Exactly.
Why would you want to change that?
Right.
But the courts have played a very active role and they've redirected the course reasonably significantly over time, but still always within that Buckley framework.
But even within that, there's been some some latitude.
But the current court, you know, as as.
Limited some certain options, on the other hand, they have emphasized other options.
So, for instance, the current court is extremely receptive to more disclosure.
Right.
And so, you know, there is some prospect about the dark money issue getting some sympathy.
It's should something like that ever reach the Supreme Court?
Not guaranteed, but in a relative sense, that's the sort of thing.
But again, that's that's not where most of the money is.
Most of the money is coming from individuals.
Right.
The only way that's likely to change is one of the key decisions in recent court cases, Citizens United being an important example.

There was another more recent case called McCutcheon, where the the the court emphatically states that independent expenditures, these are the what super PACs spend their money on political ads, give no cause for either actual or perceived corruption.
Right.
So a billion dollar ad campaign funded by a rich individual is deemed by the court not to bring forth any concerns about corruption whatsoever.
That's going back to Buckley.
But, you know, independent expenditures back in the early 70s were not a significant player.
So the world has changed.
The language of the court has not.
In fact, it's sort of doubled down on this notion that that independent expenditures cannot raise any specter of corruption or perceptions of corruption.

I think a lot of people feel challenged by that conclusion, whether the court will ever perhaps in what we call an as applied challenge saying, hey, look at the world's changed in ways you possibly didn't perceive or understand and reconsider that.
But but the fact that the court has made that statement explicitly in two major cases, if not more, even makes that a challenge.
Right.
So the the notion that that given the legal landscape right now, that there's hope of getting this particularly the large individual players out of the game is just not likely.
But I do think and I think this is a good note for us to close on.

I do think that there's a lot of power in this point of disclosure and people knowing where the money's come from and our as voters and as consumers of media, our being more astute in who is who is financing what we see.
Yeah.
And again, that that is the one opening the court has very clearly given us.
You know, Congress has put forward something called the Disclose Act.
Every Congress since then.
And it never gets through like so many other things.
And one ponders the reason why it makes for for for good political rhetoric.
Yes.
But for some reason, it just never.
Members of Congress don't want to disclose.
Well, yeah.
But but this this is something that citizens could push for.

And it is it is a way in which citizens could themselves brand candidates in the way I think many people are talking now about creating laws to require the the submission of tax returns to the public, which had been a norm is not always followed.
One could create a political norm and then put legal teeth behind it.
I mean, think about what again, think about what Taft did back in 1908.
Right.
Exactly.
Some bold move outside of the actual law actually led to changes in the law.
Yes.
Exactly.
Exactly.
Zachary, what do you think?

Do you think that that young people who are perhaps frustrated by money in politics would be motivated to at the very least get more information out there and share that information with with the public?
Yes, definitely.
I think young people are very worried about the amount of money in politics.
And I think part of the problem is that the the specter of money and the specter of of out of of hidden influence in politics turns a lot of young people away from politics.
And I think just simply making our politics more open and about the ideas and not the money is something that I think will really open politics up to a new generation of leaders.
Right.
Let me let me make one last observation along these lines.
So if you go back to the first president not to take public funding, which was President Obama back in 08, right.
But McCain did.
But since 08 to every election since the candidate that got the most money from small donors won.
Right.
And so there's a very strong recognition of the role of small donors and an emphasis on small donors.
And the technology now makes the ability to raise that kind of money so much easier.
And it turns out to be a winning strategy.
And so maybe there's some some hope in just sort of very pragmatic politics that that more candidates will see that it's not just a question of providing a rhetorical point.
But also, you know, if someone gives you a dollar, they're going to vote.
It's a mobilization strategy.
It's not necessarily a fundraising strategy or as much.
And it is a form of political speech.
I mean, we criticize we criticize that 76 Supreme Court decision, but it could actually be quite empowering for young people like Zachary to be able to give their pennies to a new kind of candidate.
Once you've given a penny, you're invested, right?
It doesn't have to fund the campaign.
